newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ANALYSTS COMMENTS ON DUTCH INTEREST RATE RISE.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS COMMENTS ON DUTCH INTEREST RATE RISE.

text.p: The Dutch central bank raised its secured loans rate to 2.50 percent from 2.00 percent and the special advances rate to 2.90 percent from 2.70 percent.
Below is a collection of analysts' comments on the move.

HAN DE JONG, ABN AMRO HOARE GOVETT: "We were a touch surprised (the special advances rate) went up by 20 basis points only. It still leaves a gap between the German repo rate (3.00 percent) and the Dutch equivalent. It would have made more sense just to close the gap today but they obviously thought 30 basis points was too much. They (the central bank) would look silly if the guilder continued to be weak.
"The central bank would probably just step into the foreign exchange market in a very discrete way."

ERIC NIENHUIS, MEESPIERSON: "It wasn't a surprise to us. It was good to close this gap between the short term interest rates (of Germany and the Netherlands). The guilder is a little bit stronger now but not much. Most parties were expecting this. The most important thing is the special advances rate. That's the marginal rate that banks borrow at. The other is more psychologically important. There's not been a big market reaction but I think it will have some impact. The hike of the secured loans rate was quite heavy."

"It really wasn't a surprise. Following the (previous) rate increase by 20 basis points...the currency did not firm...The central bank had indicated quite clearly it was uncomfortable with the recent weakness of the guilder versus the Deutschmark. If the currency stabilises...there's no need for the central bank to increase interest rates further...If it weakens further then (it) will be very quick to increase interest rates and it may increase (them) to above German rates...What they have been uncomfortable with is the weakening in the guilder since May 1996...they don't seem to have an exact number in mind..."

MARTIN LEEN, ING (RFTV INTERVIEW): "The reason why the Dutch...did not bring key rates into line with those of the Bundesbank already is that they want to see if this recent weakening of the guilder has any structural component. In the end we assess this as a first step to close the gap with Germany completely...The Netherlands is experiencing higher economic growth and higher inflation as compared to Germany and it is logical that Dutch rates are brought back in line with German rates...Differences (in Dutch and German bond yields) are expected by us to fade away...There's very little reason why the Netherlands should have lower rates anywhere across the curve."
